Pretrained models (DenseNet, ResNet, BiomedCLIP) may produce unreliable results on portable AP films out of their training distribution; model outputs for mass/nodule and pneumothorax are not trusted for this image.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph demonstrates: (1) Right-sided chest tube with pigtail configuration in the right upper hemithorax. (2) Extensive subcutaneous emphysema tracking through the soft tissues of the right chest wall, axilla, and neck/supraclavicular region. (3) Multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules and masses, with the largest measuring approximately 1.5-2 cm in the left mid-lung zone and additional nodules scattered throughout both lung fields. (4) Patchy opacities in the right mid and lower lung zones. (5) A catheter consistent with a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) is visible entering from the right upper extremity. (6) No large pleural effusion is definitively identified. Cardiac silhouette assessment is limited by overlying findings.
impression: Multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules/masses with extensive right-sided subcutaneous emphysema and right chest tube in place. The overall pattern is highly concerning for metastatic pulmonary disease complicated by air leak requiring chest tube drainage. The extensive subcutaneous emphysema may also indicate associated pneumomediastinum.
limitations: Single frontal view without lateral projection. Assessment limited by extensive subcutaneous emphysema obscuring right-sided anatomy and overlying medical devices. The pretrained models (DenseNet, ViewModel, BiomedCLIP) showed limited reliability on this image due to the unusual presentation with extensive subcutaneous emphysema and medical devices — the ViewModel gave a wrong view classification, DenseNet missed the nodules, and BiomedCLIP scores were not well-calibrated. No prior imaging available for comparison.

findings: Portable AP chest radiograph demonstrating bilateral pulmonary opacities, markedly asymmetric with right-sided predominance. The right lower lung zone shows extensive opacification obscuring the right hemidiaphragm and costophrenic angle. Patchy opacities are also present in the left lung, predominantly in the mid to lower zones. Multiple external ECG monitoring leads and wires overlie the chest. The cardiac silhouette appears enlarged but assessment is limited by AP projection. The trachea appears midline. No pneumothorax identified.
impression: Bilateral pulmonary opacities with marked right-sided predominance, consistent with multifocal pneumonia and/or ARDS. Right lower zone opacification with obscured costophrenic angle raises concern for concomitant right pleural effusion.
limitations: Single portable AP view with cardiac magnification and suboptimal lung expansion. Medical devices obscure anatomy. Pretrained models showed limited reliability (false-positive fracture, model disagreement). No lateral view available.

findings: Extensive right-sided alveolar consolidation involving the right mid and lower lung zones, with air bronchograms visible within the opacity. The consolidation obscures the right heart border and right hemidiaphragm (silhouette sign). Right costophrenic angle is blunted, suggestive of a concurrent pleural effusion. A chest tube is present, entering from the right lateral chest wall with its tip in the upper right hemithorax. The left lung is clear without focal consolidation, effusion, or pneumothorax. The left heart border is visible. The mediastinum is not widened. No acute bony abnormality is identified on this single view.
impression: Extensive right-sided alveolar consolidation with air bronchograms, consistent with right middle and lower lobe pneumonia. Right-sided pleural effusion likely present. Chest tube in situ on the right. Left lung is clear.
limitations: Single frontal view only; no lateral view available to confirm extent of pathology or quantify effusion. Cannot definitively exclude concurrent pneumothorax given chest tube presence. Model-based scores (DenseNet, ResNet) are probabilistic and should not replace clinical judgment. The BiomedCLIP model could not be loaded for zero-shot classification, limiting the available evidence. Chest tube obscures part of the right lung field. Patient positioning and potential rotation may affect interpretation.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (likely AP view). Right-sided chest tube in situ with tip directed superiorly. Right apical and lateral pneumothorax with visible visceral pleural line and absent peripheral lung markings. Multiple right-sided rib fractures (at least mid-anterior ribs). Extensive subcutaneous emphysema tracking through the right chest wall and extending superiorly into the neck soft tissues. Right mid and lower zone patchy opacity, likely representing pulmonary contusion and/or atelectasis. Right hemidiaphragm elevated. No definite right pleural effusion appreciated. Left lung field clear. Cardiac silhouette appears mildly enlarged, though assessment limited by AP projection. ECG monitoring leads and wires overlie the chest.
impression: Right-sided pneumothorax with chest tube in situ, associated with multiple right rib fractures and extensive subcutaneous emphysema. Findings consistent with significant right-sided thoracic trauma.
limitations: Single frontal view without lateral projection. AP projection magnifies cardiac silhouette and reduces sensitivity for subtle findings. Extensive monitoring leads and chest tube obscure portions of the lung fields. Pretrained model scores (DenseNet, ResNet) had low specificity (0.5-0.7 range) due to presence of chest tube and monitoring equipment, and were used only as directional corroboration. Limited assessment of posterior ribs and full extent of subcutaneous emphysema without additional views.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (likely portable AP). Right apical pneumothorax with visible visceral pleural line and absence of lung markings in the right upper zone, despite a right-sided chest tube in place with its tip oriented toward the right apex. Heterogeneous opacification in the right mid-to-lower lung zones, suggestive of atelectasis and/or consolidation. Elevated right hemidiaphragm. Surgical clips in the right perihilar region, consistent with prior thoracic surgery. Multiple ECG monitoring leads overlying the chest wall. The left lung appears clear without focal opacity, effusion, or pneumothorax. No definite rib fracture identified, though assessment is limited by overlying medical devices and single frontal projection. Cardiac silhouette is within normal limits for an AP projection.
impression: Right apical pneumothorax with chest tube in place. Right mid-to-lower zone opacification consistent with atelectasis and/or consolidation. Findings are in the setting of prior thoracic surgery (surgical clips present). The pneumothorax persists despite chest tube placement, or the tube was placed after this image was obtained.
limitations: Single portable AP projection limits evaluation. Lateral view would improve assessment of retrocardiac opacities, pleural effusion, and anterior pneumothorax. The presence of a chest tube, ECG leads, and surgical clips creates superimposed artifacts. Rib fracture cannot be definitively excluded on a single frontal view without dedicated rib series. Clinical context and comparison with prior imaging would be valuable. Pretrained models (DenseNet, ViewModel, Bone-Fracture-Detection) were evaluated and found unreliable for this specific image. BiomedCLIP provided partial corroboration but zero-shot classification is inherently uncertain.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph demonstrates a dual-lumen central venous catheter entering from the right upper chest with its tip projecting over the right upper mediastinum. There is a significant right lower lung zone opacity with ill-defined margins, obscuring the right hemidiaphragm and right costophrenic angle. The opacity appears consistent with consolidation/infiltrate with possible associated pleural effusion. The right heart border is partially obscured. The left lung is clear except for a small linear opacity in the left lower zone, likely representing subsegmental atelectasis or scarring. The left costophrenic angle is sharp. The cardiac silhouette and mediastinal contours appear within normal limits.
impression: Right lower lobe consolidation/infiltrate with probable associated small right pleural effusion. In the appropriate clinical context, pneumonia is the primary concern. Differential includes atelectasis with superimposed infection. Linear opacity in the left lower zone is nonspecific, most consistent with atelectasis.
limitations: Single frontal view limits assessment of depth and localization of the opacity. Lateral view would help differentiate anterior vs posterior pathology. The presence of a central venous catheter may limit interpretation and affects automated model performance. Automated classification models (DenseNet, BiomedCLIP) provided supporting but not definitive evidence; DenseNet was unreliable with uniformly elevated scores. Clinical correlation and comparison with prior imaging are essential.

findings: Frontal (likely portable AP) chest radiograph of a monitored patient with bilateral ECG electrodes and external lead wires. Prominent bilateral breast shadows overlie and obscure the lung bases, hemidiaphragms and costophrenic angles. The visualized aerated lung fields are clear, without focal consolidation, mass, pneumothorax or large pleural effusion; pulmonary vessels are not markedly congested. The cardiac silhouette appears prominent, consistent with AP projection magnification and body habitus; an approximate cardiothoracic ratio (a lower bound of about 0.35, limited by segmentation of the peripheral lung fields) does not support true cardiomegaly. A thin, faint line in the right paramediastinum is consistent with an external ECG monitoring lead. No definite acute cardiopulmonary abnormality is identified.
impression: No acute cardiopulmonary finding identified. The apparent basilar opacity is explained by overlying breast soft tissue, and the apparent cardiac prominence by AP (portable) projection magnification. No consolidation, effusion, pneumothorax or mass is seen on this single frontal view.
limitations: Single frontal (likely portable AP) view; no lateral view. AP projection magnifies the cardiac silhouette and lowers the diaphragm, limiting assessment of heart size and the lung bases. Large bilateral breast shadows obscure the costophrenic angles, hemidiaphragms and true lung bases, so a small pleural effusion or basilar disease cannot be excluded. Overlying ECG electrodes, lead wires and external cables cast shadows that can mimic or hide findings. The image is a quantized 8-bit PNG with a limited dynamic range. Pretrained model outputs were used only as corroboration: the multi-label classifier operating thresholds are low (nonspecific lung-opacity/infiltration flags), the cardiothoracic ratio is a segmentation-based lower bound, and zero-shot CLIP was under-confident. A very faint internal line cannot be 100 percent excluded on a single frontal view.

findings: Single frontal (AP, portable) chest radiograph of a monitored, likely intubated patient. Multiple ECG electrodes/leads and wires are present, and a tracheal tube (endotracheal tube) is seen within the midline trachea with its tip at the mid-thoracic trachea (acceptable position, above the carina; no right mainstem intubation). The right hemithorax shows diffuse hazy increased opacity, most prominent in the mid-to-lower zones, with several rounded, thin-walled lucencies in the right mid-zone; the right hemidiaphragm and right costophrenic angle are not well identified (the right base is opacified). The left hemithorax shows hazy opacity in the left base/retrocardiac region with blunting of the left costophrenic angle. The cardiac silhouette appears enlarged (apparent cardiomegaly), accentuated by the AP/supine projection. A coiled metallic density overlies the left proximal humerus (indeterminate: external monitoring hardware vs orthopedic hardware), with no definite fracture line identified. No definite pneumothorax is seen.
impression: AP portable chest radiograph of a critically ill, monitored and intubated patient showing diffuse bilateral (right greater than left) pulmonary opacification, most consistent with a combination of pleural effusion, atelectasis and consolidation (with or without pulmonary edema). The rounded lucencies in the right mid-zone are most likely aerated lung / air bronchograms within the affected right lung; a bowel-related process (e.g. diaphragmatic hernia) is a less likely alternative that cannot be excluded on a single frontal view. Apparent cardiomegaly (projection-limited). Endotracheal tube in acceptable position.
limitations: Single frontal (AP) projection only; no lateral view and no prior study for comparison. Portable/supine AP geometry exaggerates the cardiac silhouette and lower-zone opacities and makes the hemidiaphragms and costophrenic angles harder to assess. Numerous external monitoring devices (ECG leads, wires, tracheal tube) overlie and obscure parts of the lung fields and confound the pretrained models. The image is 8-bit with limited soft-tissue contrast. The exact nature of the right-mid-zone rounded lucencies is indeterminate on a single frontal view (aerated lung/air bronchograms vs a bowel-related process); a lateral view and/or cross-sectional imaging would be needed to resolve this. The left-shoulder metallic density is indeterminate (external monitoring vs orthopedic hardware). Model outputs used here (pathology classifier, zero-shot, autoencoder, segmentation) are supporting evidence only and are confounded by the external devices and the unusual right hemithorax.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (PA/AP) of an adult female (bilateral breast shadows). Both lungs are well-aerated with no focal consolidation, mass, discrete nodule, pneumothorax, or pleural effusion. The cardiomediastinal silhouette is normal in size and contour with the heart within normal limits (no cardiomegaly) and the trachea midline. Both costophrenic angles are sharp and clear. A subtle linear (subsegmental) opacity is present in the left lower lung zone, most consistent with linear atelectasis (or a band of old scarring). The right hemidiaphragm sits slightly higher than the left, a normal anatomical variant. No acute rib, clavicle, or shoulder fracture is identified.
impression: Near-normal frontal chest radiograph with no acute cardiopulmonary abnormality. The only notable finding is a subtle linear atelectasis in the left lower lung, likely incidental and benign.
limitations: Single frontal projection only (no lateral view), limiting depth localization and assessment of the posterior costophrenic angles and diaphragm. The image is grainy/low-SNR, limiting detection of subtle parenchymal opacities. Breast shadows partially obscure the lower lung zones and cardiophrenic angles. Automated model outputs were weak or discordant: a borderline DenseNet 'Infiltration'/'Fibrosis' was not corroborated by the independent ResNet classifier or by visual inspection; the ResNet 'Lung Lesion'/'Enlarged Cardiomediastinum' scores are uncalibrated 0.5 placeholders (no operating threshold) and not true signals; and the cardiothoracic ratio is only an approximation because segmentation leaked to the image border. The linear opacity cannot be fully characterized (atelectasis vs. scar) on a single frontal view.

findings: AP (portable) chest radiograph of a young child. Marked cardiomegaly: enlarged, globular cardiac silhouette with a manually measured cardiothoracic ratio of ~0.66 (above the ~0.55 AP pediatric cutoff). Diffuse bilateral hazy / interstitial opacities, perihilar and mid-to-lower zone predominant, with indistinct, blurred pulmonary vessels - a pattern of interstitial pulmonary edema / pulmonary congestion. No focal dense consolidation, no large pleural effusion, and no pneumothorax are identified. Diaphragms are high (age/position) with a gastric air bubble present; no obvious free subdiaphragmatic air. Multiple external monitoring devices overlie the chest (ECG leads, snap electrodes, coiled wires, and a small round radiopaque device over the left upper abdomen / upper chest) - these are artifacts, not pathology. No rib or clavicular fracture is seen. There is mild patient rotation.
impression: Cardiomegaly with diffuse bilateral interstitial hazy opacities - a radiographic pattern most consistent with congestive heart failure / pulmonary edema, which in a child is most commonly due to congenital heart disease or cardiomyopathy.
limitations: Single portable AP/supine view with no lateral view and no prior comparison; AP geometry and supine position magnify the heart and can overestimate the CTR. Mild patient rotation. Overlying ECG leads/electrodes and wires partially obscure the lung fields and mediastinum. The patient is a small child, outside the adult training population of the pretrained models used as sanity checks; their outputs (including a spurious 'lateral' view call and divergent cardiomegaly scores) are uncalibrated here and were used only as corroboration, not as the basis of any finding. The etiology of the cardiomegaly/edema cannot be established from a single radiograph. The small round radiopaque object over the left upper abdomen is most likely an external device, but an ingested foreign body is not definitively excluded.

findings: Portable AP frontal chest radiograph of a monitored patient bearing multiple external ECG/monitoring electrodes and support lines. There is bilateral basilar opacification, greater on the right than the left: the right basal opacity is a homogeneous density extending up to the mid-chest with a smooth, gently convex superior border, and the left base is opacified to a lesser degree; both obscure the hemidiaphragms and costophrenic angles. The upper and mid lung zones are aerated; no pneumothorax is seen. The cardiac silhouette is prominent on this AP projection, but the manually measured cardiothoracic ratio is approximately 0.39 (below the 0.5 threshold), so the heart is not clearly enlarged; the prominence is largely AP magnification plus the adjacent basilar opacity. There are hazy perihilar markings that may reflect mild interstitial edema or infiltrate. The ribs, clavicles, scapulae and spine appear intact with no definite fracture, and no definite mass or nodule is identified. No free subdiaphragmatic air is seen.
impression: Portable AP chest radiograph showing bilateral basilar opacification (right > left), most consistent with atelectasis and/or small pleural effusion in a monitored, likely supine/bedside patient. The prominent cardiac silhouette is most likely due to AP magnification (cardiothoracic ratio ~0.39; no clear cardiomegaly). Possible mild pulmonary edema/infiltrate cannot be excluded. No pneumothorax and no definite rib fracture.
limitations: Single portable AP (bedside) projection, which magnifies the heart and mediastinum and reduces sharpness; the patient is likely supine/semi-recumbent, so effusions layer posteriorly, the diaphragms ride high, and the costophrenic angles are obscured. Numerous overlying external electrodes, wires and support lines obscure parts of the lung fields, and the intravascular position of any line cannot be determined from a single frontal image. The inferior cardiac border is lost in the basilar opacity, limiting accuracy of the cardiothoracic ratio (~0.39). Effusion cannot be reliably distinguished from atelectasis on a single frontal view. Pretrained models were used as supporting evidence only: the segmentation (PSPNet) was too noisy for quantitative CTR/diaphragm measurement, the zero-shot vision-language model (BiomedCLIP) had low discrimination, and some classifier labels (Lung Opacity, Mass, Fracture) were unreliable on controls or not visually corroborated. No PA or lateral view is available for comparison.

findings: Portable AP chest radiograph. Bilateral, multifocal, patchy and hazy airspace opacities (infiltrates/patchy consolidation) are present, predominantly in the upper and mid zones of both lungs, most prominent in the right upper/mid-zone and the left perihilar/mid-zone, with relative sparing of the dependent lung bases. There is hazy retrocardiac (left lower lobe) opacity with partial obscuration of the left hemidiaphragm and left costophrenic angle. No definite pleural effusion (no meniscus), no pneumothorax, and no definite pulmonary mass or nodule. The cardiac silhouette appears widened but this is most likely AP magnification (no convincing cardiomegaly). A right-sided central venous catheter is present with its tip in the upper superior vena cava (appropriate position). A midline feeding/enteric tube passes below the diaphragm into the upper abdomen. ECG monitoring electrodes and external cables overlie the chest.
impression: Bilateral multifocal patchy/hazy airspace opacities consistent with multifocal/bilateral pneumonia (infectious infiltrate/consolidation), upper/mid-zone predominant. No convincing pulmonary edema, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, or mass. A small left pleural effusion cannot be excluded given the obscured left costophrenic angle.
limitations: Single frontal AP portable view only (no lateral view, no prior for comparison). AP geometry magnifies the cardiac silhouette (segmentation CTR 0.52 unreliable) and superimposes the scapulae over the apices. Superimposed external devices (ECG electrodes, central venous catheter, feeding tube) partially obscure the lung fields. The left hemidiaphragm/costophrenic angle is obscured by retrocardiac opacity and overlying soft tissue, so a small left pleural effusion cannot be excluded. No clinical context provided. Model support is limited: the xrv classifiers are trained mainly on PA-equivalent films (portable AP + devices are somewhat out-of-distribution), the two classifiers disagreed on consolidation/edema, MedSAM could not delineate the non-discrete infiltrate (documented negative), and BiomedCLIP is zero-shot and uncalibrated.

findings: AP (frontal) portable chest radiograph of a critically ill, intubated patient. Moderate-to-large LEFT pleural effusion: dense, homogeneous left basal/medial opacity with a concave (meniscus) upper border that obscures the left hemidiaphragm and the lower left heart border; the opacity is objectively much denser than the contralateral base and the ipsilateral upper lung. Right lung is aerated without pneumothorax, with only mild right basal haziness (mild atelectasis/effusion or positioning). Endotracheal tube lies in the trachea with its tip above the carina (approximately appropriate); central venous catheter(s) in situ; ECG monitoring electrodes on the chest wall. The patient is moderately rotated. The large radiolucent band on the left of the image is EXTERNAL air between the adducted right arm and the trunk (positioning artifact, not a pneumothorax or hyperlucent lung); a grid-like device over the left shoulder and a dense round object at the left shoulder are external monitoring hardware, not anatomy. The cardiac silhouette is not reliably assessable because of the AP projection, rotation, and the overlying left opacity.
impression: Intubated, critically ill patient whose dominant abnormality is a moderate-to-large LEFT pleural effusion, most likely with associated left lower lobe atelectasis and/or consolidation. The right lung is aerated with no pneumothorax; the endotracheal tube and central line are in acceptable position. No definite pneumothorax or other acute process is identified.
limitations: Single AP portable view (likely supine/semi-erect), with no lateral or prior comparison. Moderate patient rotation and AP projection distort the cardiac silhouette and tube positions and can mimic a mediastinal shift. The adducted right arm creates a large external air gap, and multiple external devices (ECG electrodes, shoulder hardware) overlie and obscure parts of the chest. The input is an 8-bit PNG with a fixed window and limited dynamic range. Pretrained chest-pathology classifiers (torchxrayvision DenseNet/ResNet) were degraded on this out-of-distribution image and did not corroborate the effusion, so their outputs were recorded as a negative result and not used to support any finding. The exact breakdown of the left opacity (effusion vs atelectasis vs consolidation) is uncertain, and cardiac size cannot be reliably assessed. Findings should be correlated clinically and, if the effusion is to be characterized or intervened upon, with repeat imaging or ultrasound.

findings: Portable AP chest radiograph, rotated/oblique. Bilateral lower-zone (basilar) opacities, more extensive on the right (aerated lung extends only to the mid-lung) than on the left (basilar opacity). A left pleural pigtail drainage catheter is in situ over the left lower chest, the pigtail tip coiled, with the tube exiting the left lateral chest wall. Enlarged cardiomediastinal silhouette. Multiple external ECG monitoring leads and a thin left paramediastinal line (most likely an external ECG lead). Trachea patent, roughly midline. No pneumothorax, no acute rib fracture, no apical disease, and no discrete pulmonary mass or nodule.
impression: Bilateral basilar opacities (right more extensive than left) with a left pleural pigtail drainage catheter in situ and an enlarged cardiomediastinal silhouette on a rotated portable AP film - most consistent with bilateral pleural effusion(s) ± atelectasis/consolidation (± cardiogenic pulmonary edema), the left collection drained via the pigtail catheter.
limitations: Single rotated portable AP view with no PA/lateral view and no prior comparison; AP projection magnifies the heart and reduces penetration; supine/semi-upright positioning causes effusions to layer posteriorly (hazy basilar opacification) rather than form a meniscus, limiting separation of effusion from atelectasis/consolidation; overlying ECG leads and tubes can mimic or mask pathology; the cardiac silhouette blends with the adjacent opacities, limiting assessment of true heart size and the exact extent/laterality of the opacities; pretrained pathology-model scores do not laterlize and are sensitive to the overlying artifacts (used only as corroboration).

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. A right chest-wall implantable venous access port (reservoir) is present, with its catheter forming a prominent loop in the right upper chest and the tip projecting over the superior vena cava; a folded/redundant catheter segment is seen at the reservoir. Multiple surgical clips overlie the left mid-lung and left paracardiac region, and a small metallic clip is present in the left upper mediastinum. A cluster of 4-5 rounded soft-tissue opacities (approximately 1-2 cm each) projects over the right lower lobe, above the right hemidiaphragm. A rounded, somewhat prominent left hilar/perihilar opacity is noted. The cardiac silhouette is moderate (cardiothoracic ratio approximately 0.52, borderline). No pleural effusion, pneumothorax, or focal consolidation is identified; both costophrenic angles are sharp.
impression: Multiple rounded nodular opacities in the right lower lobe with a prominent left hilar opacity, in a patient with an indwelling port and prior surgical clips. Most concerning for multiple pulmonary nodules/lymphadenopathy (metastatic disease is a consideration given the port; granulomatous or inflammatory etiologies are also possible), warranting CT chest for characterization. No acute cardiopulmonary process (no effusion, pneumothorax, or consolidation).
limitations: Single frontal projection (no lateral view); PA vs AP is uncertain, affecting cardiac-size assessment (CT ratio ~0.52 is borderline) and characterization of hilar/mediastinal structures. The right-lower rounded opacity cluster cannot be definitively distinguished as pulmonary nodules versus mediastinal/pericardial lymphadenopathy on a single frontal view - CT is required. The catheter loop and the radiopaque band below the port reservoir are device-related and not fully characterizable (coiling vs malposition). 8-bit PNG conversion limits subtle low-contrast detail. No prior studies for comparison. Model-based pathology screening may be perturbed by the hardware; the PadChest-only variant over-called effusion/pneumonia that were not visually confirmed. Clinical history (e.g., indication for the port) is unavailable.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (frontal view confirmed with 0.994 model probability) of an adolescent/young-adult female. A well-defined, smooth, rounded soft-tissue opacity (approximately 4.5-5.5 cm) is present in the left perihilar/mediastinal region, forming a second contour on the left heart border with a sharp margin against aerated lung; segmentation and classifier evidence indicate it is separate from the cardiac silhouette and the heart itself is not clearly enlarged (approximate cardiothoracic ratio ~0.25, a lower bound). A small (approximately 1.2-1.6 cm) rounded opacity with a slightly lucent center is seen in the lateral left lower lung zone (small nodule vs bulla). A cluster of irregular metallic densities overlies the C2-C3 cervical region just below the mandible, with a pattern that could represent dental work or a metallic foreign body/retained fragments. The remaining lung fields are well aerated with no consolidation, pleural effusion, or pneumothorax; costophrenic angles are sharp; both hemidiaphragms are smooth with no subdiaphragmatic free air; the visualised bony thorax (ribs, clavicles, scapulae, spine) appears intact.
impression: Left perihilar/mediastinal mass. The dominant abnormality is a well-defined rounded soft-tissue mass in the left perihilar/mediastinal region that is distinct from a non-enlarged heart, in a young female. The leading differential is a mediastinal/perihilar mass (e.g. lymphoma, bronchogenic cyst, neurogenic tumour, thymic or germ-cell tumour); a vascular anomaly/prominent pulmonary artery is not excluded on a single frontal view. Secondary findings are a small left lower-zone rounded opacity and a cervical metallic density cluster (dental vs foreign body). CT of the chest is recommended to characterise the mass.
limitations: Single frontal view only (no lateral view), so the mass cannot be assigned to an anterior/middle/posterior mediastinal compartment and a purely vascular origin cannot be fully excluded. The patient is likely an adolescent/young-adult female, so adult reference values (e.g. cardiothoracic ratio, vascular sizes) do not fully apply. Pretrained-model outputs (DenseNet/ResNet pathology classifiers, BiomedCLIP zero-shot, PSPNet segmentation) are corroborating only, not diagnostic; the models were trained mainly on adult chest radiographs and the classifiers disagree in magnitude, and the PSPNet-derived cardiothoracic ratio is a lower bound due to heart-mask under-segmentation. The cervical metallic densities cannot be definitively classified as dental work versus a foreign body on this image. The input is a PNG re-save with fixed contrast.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. Bilateral diffuse reticulonodular and patchy airspace (interstitial-alveolar) pulmonary opacities, most marked in the mid and lower zones, partially obscuring the cardiac silhouette and the left hemidiaphragm. The left costophrenic angle is obscured by basilar haziness (a small pleural effusion or basilar atelectasis/consolidation cannot be excluded); the right costophrenic angle is relatively preserved. No pneumothorax. A 2x3 grid of metallic surgical clips is projected over the right mid-lung field (implanted hardware from prior surgery, not a mass). A mandibular reconstruction plate is present in the jaw region; ECG electrode markers are projected over both lateral chest walls; a small metallic clip is seen over the right shoulder. The cardiac silhouette is indeterminate (not clearly enlarged); the mediastinum is not widened; no endotracheal, nasogastric or central venous catheter is visualized. No displaced rib fracture is seen.
impression: Bilateral diffuse pulmonary opacities (reticulonodular/patchy interstitial-alveolar pattern), most consistent with pulmonary edema or multifocal pneumonia/infiltrates; a small left pleural effusion cannot be excluded. No pneumothorax. Multiple external monitoring devices and implanted hardware (mandibular plate, ECG electrodes, surgical clips) are present.
limitations: Single frontal view only - no lateral view and no prior images for comparison; 8-bit PNG without DICOM metadata (patient data, projection and exposure parameters unavailable). AP versus PA projection is uncertain (a view classifier confirms frontal but not AP/PA), which limits assessment of cardiac size, a finding further obscured by the diffuse opacities (cardiac silhouette indeterminate). Multiple superimposed metallic/external objects (mandibular plate, ECG electrodes, surgical clips, shoulder clip, corner marker) cause blooming and may obscure underlying anatomy; the surgical clips overlap the right lung field. The diffuse opacities themselves reduce contrast of the cardiac borders and costophrenic angles, so a small effusion cannot be definitively confirmed or excluded. Model-based readings are supportive but not definitive: DenseNet and ResNet disagree on fine-grained labels, BiomedCLIP is zero-shot and uncalibrated, and the metallic objects are partly out-of-distribution for these models (mitigated by a metal-suppressed re-run that left the scores unchanged). The distinction between edema and infection cannot be resolved from a single radiograph.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (likely AP/supine) of a hospitalized patient with multiple indwelling devices: a right-sided central venous catheter (looping, with a connector/anchor), a ring-shaped radiopaque device overlying the right mid-lung, a small surgical clip, and ECG electrodes. There are diffuse bilateral pulmonary opacities, most pronounced in the mid and lower lung zones, with a patchy interstitial-alveolar (consolidation) pattern that is asymmetric and most dense at the left base (near-complete opacification). Costophrenic angles are blunted/obscured (possible small pleural effusions). No definite pneumothorax, no discrete pulmonary nodule or mass, and no definite cardiomegaly (the cardiac silhouette is obscured by overlying opacity).
impression: Diffuse bilateral, lower-zone-predominant pulmonary opacities with a left-base consolidation in a patient with indwelling lines - most consistent with multifocal pneumonia (including aspiration) and/or pulmonary edema.
limitations: Single frontal view only (no lateral). Likely AP/supine projection, over-penetrated and low-contrast; multiple indwelling devices (catheter, ring device, clips, ECG electrodes) obscure the lung fields and mediastinum. The cardiac silhouette and costophrenic angles are obscured, so cardiac size and effusions cannot be reliably assessed. Pretrained model outputs (DenseNet/ResNet) were used only as corroboration of visible findings; Mass/Nodule scores and some threshold-pinned labels were discounted as device/threshold artifacts. The asymmetric (left > right) consolidation pattern favors pneumonia/aspiration, but pulmonary edema cannot be excluded.

findings: Portable anteroposterior (AP), supine chest radiograph of a monitored patient with multiple ECG electrodes, external monitoring cables, and a right-sided central venous catheter whose tip lies in the region of the superior vena cava. Diffuse bilateral airspace and interstitial opacities are present, more extensive on the right than the left, with basal and perihilar predominance and relative apical sparing; there is confluent consolidation in the right mid-to-lower zone with obscuration of the right heart border and right hemidiaphragm. The left mid-to-lower zone shows reticular and patchy airspace opacities with a hazy left base. No pneumothorax is identified and no endotracheal tube is seen. The cardiomediastinal silhouette is prominent, exaggerated by the AP projection; marked cardiomegaly is not demonstrated.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (left side marker present). findings: Frontal chest radiograph. findings: Frontal (AP, likely portable/ICU) chest radiograph with an R marker. Extensive subcutaneous emphysema: streaky air-density gas tracking through the right neck, axilla and upper chest wall. findings: Frontal chest radiograph (frontal projection confirmed, 99.8%). Source is an 8-bit PNG (reduced dynamic range). The left heart border and left hemidiaphragm are obscured by the opacity, limiting cardiac-size and diaphragmatic assessment (CTR ~0.51 likely an underestimate).
